# Savings realisation: identified versus landed

A small working model of the one number a cloud-savings business has to be able
to defend: how much of what we identified actually showed up in the customer's
bill, and where the rest went.

**All figures here are synthetic**, generated by `savings_realisation.py` from a
fixed seed. I have no access to anyone's real spend and have not guessed at it.
The method is the deliverable.

## Why this and not a dashboard

A dashboard shows the number moved. Finance has to say why, to someone who will
act on the answer. That means three things a chart does not do on its own:

1. **Close the bridge.** Identified splits into actioned and backlog; actioned
   splits into realised and leakage. Both identities are asserted in the
   self-check, so the bridge cannot silently stop adding up.
2. **Separate the two causes.** A movement in realised savings is either volume
   (customers approved more work) or rate (the same work converted differently).
   Those have different owners. Volume is a customer-success question. Rate is a
   product question. Reporting one number hides which one you have.
3. **Stop at what is material.** $25,000 or a 15% miss, top five only, the rest
   aggregated to one line. Commentary nobody reads is commentary nobody acts on.

## The three gaps, and who owns each

| Gap | Definition | Usually owned by |
|---|---|---|
| Backlog | Identified, never actioned | The customer, pending approval |
| Leakage | Actioned, but the bill moved less | The product |
| Drift | Bill moved, then crept back up | Nobody, which is the problem |

Drift is not modelled here because it needs a time series of the bill after the
action, which I do not have. I have left it named rather than quietly dropped,
because it is the gap most likely to be invisible internally.

## Rate and volume, and one honest caveat

Volume is isolated by holding conversion at the prior period, and rate is the
remainder. That folds the cross term into rate, so the two parts always add back
to the total. The alternative is a three-way split with a residual nobody can
explain in a meeting. I would rather have two numbers that reconcile than three
that do not. The self-check asserts the add-back.

## Run it

```
python3 savings_realisation.py          # writes report.md and realisation.csv
python3 savings_realisation.py --test   # self-check
```

The self-check asserts that both bridges close for every row, that the rate and
volume split adds back to the total movement, that a period compared against
itself produces exactly zero variance, and that commentary is deterministic and
ordered by shortfall.

## Where this comes from

I run budget versus actual for a USD 1.1m technology programme at Illumina's
Bengaluru centre: committed against actual across cost centres and projects,
variance analysis, and the commentary that goes with it. The shape of the
problem is the same one here. The subject matter is cloud spend rather than a
programme budget, and I would need your data and a conversation to say anything
real about the second.
